cards.title: The ML Platform Concept — Paved Roads for ML Teams
cards.teaser: An ML platform is not a single tool — it is an opinionated, integrated set of infrastructure and services that gives ML teams a paved road from raw data to deployed model, eliminating the need to wire together ad-hoc tooling for every project.

runs.text: Without a platform, every ML team at a large organization independently solves the same infrastructure problems: how do we access features consistently, track experiments, version models, schedule training jobs, and serve predictions? The result is a sprawl of incompatible solutions — some using SageMaker, some using custom scripts on EC2, some using Airflow, none sharing anything.
An ML platform provides:

items.text: A feature store
— consistent, reusable feature definitions shared across teams and preventing training-serving skew.
Experiment tracking
— centralized logging of runs, metrics, hyperparameters, and artifacts so experiments are reproducible and comparable.
Model registry
— a versioned store of trained models with metadata about training data, performance, and approval status.
Training orchestration
— scalable compute for distributed training, with job scheduling and resource isolation.
Serving infrastructure
— standardized online and batch serving with built-in autoscaling, canary rollouts, and monitoring.

runs.text: The "paved road" metaphor — popularized by Netflix — captures the intent: the platform makes the right way the easy way. An ML engineer who follows the platform gets experiment tracking, reproducibility, and monitoring for free. Going off-road is allowed but immediately more expensive.

Platforms don't eliminate ML complexity — they push it down into infrastructure so individual teams can focus on model quality rather than plumbing. The key success metric for a platform team is reduction in "time to first deployed model" for a new ML team.
An ML platform is the shared infrastructure that makes it easy to train, track, deploy, and monitor models — so each ML team doesn't have to build those same foundations from scratch.

cards.title: Build vs Buy — When In-House Pays Off vs When SaaS Wins
cards.teaser: Building a custom ML platform costs tens of millions in engineering time and takes 2–3 years to mature. The decision hinges on scale, differentiation, data gravity, and how many ML teams you have.

runs.text: The build-vs-buy decision for an ML platform is not primarily about capability — by 2026, SaaS platforms (SageMaker, Vertex AI, Azure ML, Databricks) cover nearly all standard MLOps needs. The decision is about three things: data gravity, differentiation, and critical mass.
Arguments for building in-house:

items.text: Scale beyond vendor limits.
Uber, Airbnb, and Netflix run thousands of ML models. At that scale, per-API-call pricing and vendor-imposed quotas create both cost and operational risk that custom infrastructure avoids.
Deep integration with proprietary data systems.

When your data lives in a bespoke data warehouse or requires custom access controls, SaaS connectors may not suffice. Michelangelo was built specifically to integrate tightly with Uber's Hive and Kafka infrastructure.
ML is a core competency.
Companies where ML is a primary product differentiator (ranking, pricing, recommendations as the product) benefit from platform-level control unavailable in SaaS.
Regulatory/data-sovereignty requirements.
Some industries (finance, healthcare, defense) cannot send training data to public cloud ML services even encrypted.

runs.text: Arguments for buying SaaS:

items.text: Fewer than 20 ML engineers.
Below this threshold, maintaining a platform costs more in engineering time than it saves. The platform team will be perpetually under-resourced relative to the ML teams it serves.
Speed to market.
SaaS platforms are available immediately. An in-house platform takes 18–36 months to reach feature parity with mature commercial offerings.
ML is not the core product.
If ML is enabling the product rather than being the product, the investment in bespoke infrastructure rarely pays off.

runs.text: The most common mistake: starting with a custom build before proving ML ROI. Build the platform after your 10th model is in production, not before your first. Many in-house platform initiatives have been abandoned after 18 months because the ML investment never materialized.

Build when you have hundreds of models, proprietary data infrastructure, and ML as a core differentiator. Buy when you're just getting started, have fewer than 20 ML engineers, or ML is not your main business.

cards.title: Uber Michelangelo — The Seminal In-House Platform
cards.teaser: Uber's Michelangelo, described in a 2017 engineering blog post, set the template for what an internal ML platform should be: an end-to-end system covering data management, training, evaluation, deployment, and monitoring, unified across the entire company.

runs.text: In September 2017, Uber Engineering published "Meet Michelangelo: Uber's Machine Learning Platform" (eng.uber.com/michelangelo-machine-learning-platform/). The post described a system that had been running in production for two years and was supporting thousands of engineers across dozens of use cases including surge pricing, ETA estimation, and fraud detection.
What Michelangelo standardized:

items.text: Feature management

— a shared feature store so that "driver acceptance rate over the last 30 minutes" is computed once and reused across all models that need it, preventing both duplicate computation and training-serving skew.
Training pipeline
— declarative training jobs on a distributed Spark cluster. Engineers specify the model type, features, and target; the platform handles compute scheduling and hyperparameter search.
Evaluation framework
— standardized offline evaluation with automatic generation of performance reports, enabling apples-to-apples model comparisons.
Model serving
— a unified serving system with sub-100ms latency, handling both online (real-time) and offline (batch) scoring.
Online monitoring
— automatic drift detection comparing training distributions to live prediction distributions.

runs.text: The key architectural insight of Michelangelo was treating the entire ML workflow as a first-class software engineering problem: versioned, testable, reproducible. Before Michelangelo, Uber's ML models were ad-hoc scripts with no standardized path from experiment to production. After, deploying a new model was a configuration change rather than a new engineering project.

The Michelangelo post is required reading for any engineer designing an ML platform. Its core argument — that ML infrastructure diversity is expensive and that standardization pays for itself — has been validated at every company that has followed its pattern.

Michelangelo was Uber's answer to having too many teams solving the same ML infrastructure problem independently. It unified feature management, training, evaluation, serving, and monitoring into one system everyone could use.

cards.title: Airbnb Bighead — The Early Standardization Story
cards.teaser: Airbnb's Bighead preceded many open-source MLOps tools and showed how a mid-size company (not Uber's scale) could still benefit enormously from a unified ML platform — with a focus on reducing time-to-production for new models.

runs.text: Airbnb's ML platform, called Bighead, was described in a series of engineering blog posts starting in 2018. Like Michelangelo, it was built in response to the same problem: ML teams were maintaining incompatible individual pipelines, making model reuse and operational handoffs difficult.
Bighead's distinctive contributions:

items.text: DAG-based ML pipeline definition
— Bighead represented the full model pipeline (data ingestion, feature engineering, training, evaluation) as a directed acyclic graph, enabling reproducibility and incremental re-runs.
Zipline feature store
— Airbnb open-sourced their feature computation framework as Zipline (later Chronon), which became one of the first public feature store implementations.
Unified model interface

— Bighead required all models to implement a standard Python interface for training and prediction, enabling the serving layer to handle heterogeneous model types (sklearn, XGBoost, TensorFlow) uniformly.
Notebook-friendly development
— Engineers developed models in Jupyter notebooks and could "graduate" those notebooks into production pipelines through Bighead tooling, without a full rewrite.

runs.text: Bighead's early standardization story is instructive because Airbnb built it before the current generation of open-source MLOps tools (MLflow, Kubeflow, Feast) existed. Many of the abstractions they invented independently — pipeline DAGs, feature stores, model registries — became the foundational primitives of those open-source projects.

By 2022, Airbnb had significantly shifted toward open-source tooling (MLflow, Airflow) for components where commercial and open-source alternatives had matured, retaining proprietary components only where deep Airbnb-specific integration was required. This arc — build, share the abstractions, migrate to open-source implementations — is a common pattern for large-company ML platforms.

Bighead was Airbnb's internal ML platform that invented many abstractions (feature stores, pipeline DAGs, model interfaces) that later became standard in the open-source world. It showed that standardization pays even at mid-scale.

cards.title: Netflix Metaflow — Python-First and Now Open-Source
cards.teaser: Netflix's Metaflow was designed around a core insight: data scientists write Python, and the platform should work with that grain rather than against it. Now open-source, it provides a decorator-based workflow system that scales from a laptop to AWS without code changes.

runs.text: Netflix published Metaflow in 2019 and open-sourced it the same year (github.com/Netflix/metaflow). Unlike Michelangelo and Bighead, which were primarily built by and for infrastructure engineers, Metaflow was explicitly designed to be used directly by data scientists — people who write Python, not Kubernetes YAML.
Metaflow's key design choices:

items.text: Python decorators as infrastructure API
— adding
@resources(cpu=4, gpu=1)
to a step requests that compute. Adding
@retry(times=3)
makes the step retry on failure. Infrastructure concerns are expressed in Python, not in separate configuration files.
Local-to-cloud execution parity
— the same Metaflow script runs identically on a laptop (using local compute) and in AWS (using EC2/Batch). The data scientist's development loop is not broken when scaling up.
Versioned data artifacts
— every step's output is automatically versioned and persisted. Any run can be resumed from any step, and any artifact from any past run can be retrieved by run ID.
S3 as the universal data layer
— Metaflow checkpoints all intermediate results to S3 (or equivalent object storage), making distributed execution seamless without requiring a separate artifact store.

runs.text: Metaflow does not replace a full ML platform — it handles workflow definition and execution but deliberately punts on feature stores and model serving, integrating with external systems for those. Its focus is narrow and opinionated: make the training-side workflow seamless for data scientists.

Metaflow is now maintained by Outerbounds (founded by the original Netflix Metaflow team) with an open-source core and a commercial managed platform. It has been adopted widely beyond Netflix, including by several major financial institutions where its Python-native approach appeals to quant teams.

Metaflow lets data scientists write ordinary Python code, with decorators to request cloud compute and automatic versioning of all data. It bridges laptop development and production cloud execution without requiring a rewrite.

cards.title: Databricks — Spark-Native, Lakehouse-Aligned
cards.teaser: Databricks started as managed Spark-on-cloud and evolved into a unified analytics and ML platform centered on the lakehouse architecture. Its strength is when training data lives in Delta Lake and the team is already Spark-fluent.

runs.text: Databricks occupies a distinct position in the ML platform landscape: it is simultaneously a data engineering platform, a feature engineering environment, and an ML training and serving platform. Its coherence comes from the lakehouse architecture — data stored in Delta Lake (open-source, Parquet + transaction log) is accessible by both ETL pipelines and ML training jobs without movement or duplication.
Key Databricks ML platform components:

items.text: MLflow (originated at Databricks)

— experiment tracking, model registry, and serving. MLflow was open-sourced by Databricks in 2018 and became the de facto standard for experiment tracking across the industry, used far outside Databricks itself.
Feature Store
— integrated with Delta Lake, enabling point-in-time correct feature lookups and automatic feature lineage tracking.
AutoML
— glass-box AutoML that generates Python notebooks showing what it tried, making it useful for prototyping even when the AutoML result itself isn't used in production.
Model Serving
— serverless real-time serving with sub-100ms p99 latency, supporting MLflow models, Python functions, and LLM endpoints.
Unity Catalog integration
— governance and lineage for models and features alongside data assets, providing a single governance plane for the entire data + ML estate.

runs.text: Databricks is the strongest choice when the organization has significant data engineering investment already in Spark/Delta. The ML platform is most powerful when training data is already in Delta Lake — the "gravity" of data shapes platform choice, and Databricks wins where data gravity points to the lakehouse.

Its relative weakness is infrastructure flexibility: Databricks runs on Databricks compute. Teams that need to train on custom GPU clusters, or deploy to on-premises edge hardware, find the platform's compute abstraction too constraining.

Databricks is the ML platform for teams already living in the Spark/Delta lakehouse world. Training data, features, experiments, models, and serving all live in one place, unified by the lakehouse architecture.

cards.title: AWS SageMaker — The Broad AWS-Native Suite
cards.teaser: SageMaker is the most feature-complete managed ML platform in public cloud — covering everything from data labeling to inference at the edge — but its breadth comes at the cost of complexity, and its abstraction model can feel leaky when things go wrong.

runs.text: Amazon SageMaker, launched in 2017, is a collection of services unified under a single brand. By 2026 it covers essentially every stage of the ML lifecycle, including:

items.text: SageMaker Studio
— IDE for notebooks, experiments, and pipeline visualization.
SageMaker Data Wrangler and Feature Store
— no-code/low-code feature engineering and a managed feature store with online (DynamoDB-backed) and offline (S3) stores.
SageMaker Training
— managed training on any EC2 instance type, with support for distributed training (SageMaker Distributed), hyperparameter tuning (SageMaker Experiments), and spot instances.
SageMaker Pipelines
— CI/CD-style ML pipelines with a Python SDK for defining DAG workflows. Natively integrated with CloudWatch, CodePipeline, and EventBridge.
SageMaker Endpoint / Serverless Inference
— managed real-time serving with autoscaling, A/B testing, and multi-model endpoints for cost-efficient hosting of many small models.
SageMaker Model Monitor
— drift detection and data quality monitoring on live endpoints.

runs.text: SageMaker is the default choice for AWS-native organizations, especially those using other AWS services for data (S3, Redshift, Glue). The IAM integration and VPC networking mean that existing AWS security posture extends naturally to ML workloads.
Known friction points:

items.text: Debugging training failures
requires navigating CloudWatch logs, which are verbose and fragmented across log groups.
Local development parity
— the
sagemaker.LocalSession()
mode exists but requires Docker and has inconsistencies with cloud behavior.
Pricing complexity
— SageMaker charges separately for notebooks, training, endpoints, Feature Store reads/writes, and pipelines. Cost optimization requires careful configuration.

runs.text: SageMaker is AWS's all-in-one ML platform. It covers every step from data labeling to edge deployment, integrates naturally with other AWS services, and is the right choice if you're already committed to the AWS ecosystem.

cards.title: GCP Vertex AI — Google's Unified Platform
cards.teaser: Vertex AI is Google's consolidation of its previously fragmented ML offerings (AI Platform, AutoML, AI Hub) into a single unified platform — backed by Google's TPU infrastructure and tightly integrated with BigQuery as the data layer.

runs.text: Google launched Vertex AI in 2021 to replace its fragmented collection of ML products. The unification addressed a real problem: Google had AutoML (for no-code model training), AI Platform (for custom training), AI Hub (for model sharing), and Cloud ML Engine — all overlapping, with inconsistent APIs. Vertex AI provides a single entry point.
Vertex AI's distinctive strengths:

items.text: TPU access
— Google's Tensor Processing Units are available only through GCP. For large language model training and inference, TPUv4/v5 pods provide price-performance that GPU clusters cannot match.
BigQuery ML integration
— SQL-native model training and inference directly in BigQuery, useful for organizations whose analysts are SQL-fluent but not Python-fluent.
Vertex AI Pipelines
— built on Kubeflow Pipelines (KFP) SDK, providing portability between Vertex AI managed pipelines and self-hosted KFP clusters.
Model Garden
— a curated catalog of foundation models (Gemini, PaLM, and third-party models) with one-click deployment to Vertex AI endpoints.
Feature Store and Matching Engine
— managed feature serving with low-latency reads, plus Matching Engine for approximate nearest-neighbor search (vector search for embeddings).

runs.text: Vertex AI is the natural home for organizations with data in BigQuery, teams running large-scale deep learning that could benefit from TPUs, or organizations building LLM-powered applications on Google's foundation model stack. Its weakness is that outside the GCP-native data ecosystem, it offers less advantage over SageMaker or Databricks.

Vertex AI is Google's consolidated ML platform — one place for AutoML, custom training on TPUs, pipelines, model serving, and access to Google's foundation models. It's strongest when your data is already in BigQuery.

cards.title: Azure ML — Microsoft's Offering
cards.teaser: Azure Machine Learning is Microsoft's managed ML platform, differentiated by deep enterprise integration (Active Directory, RBAC, Azure DevOps), first-class support for responsible AI tooling, and the tightest integration with Microsoft's broader data estate (Synapse, Fabric, Power BI).

runs.text: Azure ML is the enterprise-focused ML platform in the big-three cloud landscape. While SageMaker and Vertex AI attract ML-native organizations, Azure ML's adoption is often driven by existing Microsoft enterprise commitments — organizations already running Azure DevOps, Active Directory, and Synapse Analytics for data find Azure ML the path of least resistance.
Distinctive Azure ML capabilities:

items.text: Responsible AI dashboard
— integrated fairness analysis, error analysis, model explainability (SHAP, LIME), and causal inference. Microsoft has invested more in responsible AI tooling than any other platform vendor.
Azure ML Pipelines
— YAML-defined or SDK-defined pipelines with reusable components, native integration with Azure DevOps for CI/CD, and event-driven triggering via Azure Event Grid.
Managed endpoints
— online endpoints (real-time) and batch endpoints, both with blue/green deployment, traffic splitting, and native Azure Monitor integration.
Azure OpenAI Service integration
— Azure ML is the orchestration layer for organizations combining fine-tuned models with Azure OpenAI, enabling hybrid deployment patterns.
Enterprise RBAC and compliance
— workspace-level access control integrated with Azure Active Directory. Audit logs flow to Azure Monitor and Log Analytics. Supports HIPAA, SOC 2, and FedRAMP compliance frameworks.

runs.text: Azure ML's position has strengthened significantly with Microsoft Fabric (2023) providing a unified data + analytics platform. With Fabric's OneLake as the storage layer, Azure ML can now access all organizational data assets through a single governance model, a story that now rivals Databricks' lakehouse integration.

Azure ML is Microsoft's ML platform with the strongest enterprise integration story — Active Directory, DevOps pipelines, compliance tooling, and responsible AI features built in. It's the natural choice for Microsoft-stack organizations.

cards.title: Platform Comparison — SageMaker vs Vertex AI vs Azure ML vs Databricks vs DIY Kubeflow
cards.teaser: No platform dominates across all criteria. The right choice depends on data gravity, cloud commitment, team composition, and whether the organization is optimizing for breadth of features or depth of integration.

runs.text: A structured comparison across five dimensions — training, feature store, serving, pipeline orchestration, and governance:

items.text: SageMaker (AWS)

— training: broadest instance type selection including Inferentia/Trainium chips; feature store: managed online + offline with S3/DynamoDB; serving: multi-model endpoints, real-time and serverless; pipelines: native Pipelines SDK, integrates with Step Functions; governance: IAM + CloudTrail. Best for: AWS-native orgs, broad ML use cases.
Vertex AI (GCP)

— training: TPU pods for large models, strong AutoML; feature store: managed with low-latency serving + Bigtable backing; serving: dedicated + shared endpoints, Matching Engine for vectors; pipelines: KFP-based, portable; governance: Dataplex integration. Best for: BigQuery data gravity, LLM workloads, TPU training.
Azure ML (Microsoft)

— training: AzureML compute clusters, supports NDv4 (A100); feature store: newer, maturing; serving: managed online/batch endpoints; pipelines: SDK v2 YAML pipelines, Azure DevOps integration; governance: Responsible AI dashboard, AAD RBAC. Best for: enterprise Microsoft shops, regulated industries.
Databricks

— training: Spark distributed + GPU clusters; feature store: Delta-backed, point-in-time correct; serving: serverless model serving via MLflow; pipelines: Delta Live Tables + Jobs; governance: Unity Catalog. Best for: Spark/Delta data teams, lakehouse-centric orgs.
DIY Kubeflow stack

— training: Kubernetes Training Operator (TFJob, PyTorchJob); feature store: Feast (open-source); serving: KServe (Knative-based); pipelines: KFP or Argo Workflows; governance: custom. Best for: multi-cloud or on-prem requirements, maximum control, large platform team.

runs.text: Key decision heuristics:

items.text: Data gravity wins.
The platform co-located with your data almost always beats a better platform that requires data movement. 80% of platform decisions should follow data location.
Feature store maturity matters.

If low-latency feature serving at inference time is critical, Vertex AI and SageMaker's managed feature stores are production-ready; Azure ML's is newer. Databricks wins on offline features; Feast DIY requires more operational work.
LLM workloads favor Vertex AI or Databricks.
TPU access and Model Garden (Vertex) or MLflow + GPU clusters (Databricks) currently provide the best price-performance for large-scale foundation model work.

runs.text: Choose the platform where your data already lives. SageMaker for AWS, Vertex AI for GCP + BigQuery, Azure ML for Microsoft enterprise, Databricks for lakehouse/Spark teams, DIY Kubeflow if you need multi-cloud or on-prem with a large platform team to support it.

cards.title: The Open-Source DIY Stack — Kubeflow + MLflow + Feast + KServe
cards.teaser: A DIY ML platform assembled from open-source components gives maximum control and cloud portability — but requires a dedicated platform team to operate. Each component is production-ready; the integration work is where the real effort lives.

runs.text: For organizations with multi-cloud requirements, on-premises infrastructure, or strong vendor-independence policies, the open-source stack provides a viable path to a production ML platform. The canonical DIY stack as of 2026:

items.text: Kubeflow

— ML workflow orchestration on Kubernetes. Provides KFP (pipeline SDK), the Training Operator (distributed training), and Notebooks (JupyterHub-based). Runs on any Kubernetes cluster: EKS, GKE, AKS, or bare metal.
MLflow

— experiment tracking, model registry, and serving. The most widely adopted open-source MLOps tool; integrates with nearly every training framework. Can be self-hosted on a VM or Kubernetes, or used as Databricks-managed MLflow.
Feast

— open-source feature store. Supports multiple online stores (Redis, DynamoDB, Bigtable) and offline stores (Parquet, BigQuery, Redshift). Defines features in Python; materializes from offline to online on a schedule.
KServe

— Kubernetes-native model serving built on Knative. Supports multi-framework inference (TensorFlow, PyTorch, SKLearn, XGBoost, custom), serverless autoscaling to zero, and canary rollouts via traffic splitting.

runs.text: Integration patterns:

items.text: Argo Workflows or Airflow
often supplements KFP for non-training DAGs (data prep, batch scoring).
MinIO or object storage
provides the artifact backend for MLflow and KFP pipeline artifacts.
Prometheus + Grafana
for infrastructure and serving metrics; Evidently AI or WhyLogs for ML-specific drift monitoring.

runs.text: The DIY stack's hidden cost is upgrades. Each component has its own release cycle, and Kubeflow + MLflow + Feast + KServe version compatibility is not guaranteed. A dedicated platform engineer must own the upgrade path. Budget at least one full-time engineer per 20 ML engineers using the platform.

The DIY open-source ML stack assembles Kubeflow for pipelines, MLflow for tracking and registry, Feast for features, and KServe for serving. It's cloud-portable and vendor-independent — but you own the integration and upgrades.

cards.title: Platform Engineering for ML — IDP Patterns Applied to ML
cards.teaser: Platform engineering for ML applies the same Internal Developer Platform (IDP) principles used in software engineering — golden paths, self-service, opinionated defaults — to the ML workflow. The ML platform IS an IDP, purpose-built for the ML developer experience.

runs.text: The platform engineering discipline (popularized by the CNCF's Platform Engineering whitepaper and Humanitec's State of Platform Engineering reports) defines an Internal Developer Platform as the set of tools, services, and workflows that abstract infrastructure complexity for application developers. Applied to ML:

items.text: Golden paths

— the platform provides a blessed end-to-end workflow for the most common ML patterns (tabular classification, time-series forecasting, NLP fine-tuning). Following the golden path gives you monitoring, CI/CD, and governance for free.
Self-service provisioning

— an ML engineer creates a new project, registers a feature group, spins up a training cluster, or deploys a model without raising a ticket. The platform exposes these as self-service APIs or UI workflows.
Opinionated defaults with escape hatches

— the platform has a default framework (e.g., PyTorch), a default experiment tracker (MLflow), a default serving runtime (KServe). Teams can override defaults but must explicitly opt out and own the operational consequences.
Developer experience as a first-class concern
— the platform team measures "time to first model in production" and "time to reproduce a historical experiment" as primary success metrics, not just infrastructure uptime.

runs.text: A critical IDP pattern for ML is the
contract-based interface

: the platform defines a standard model packaging format (MLflow model, ONNX, or a custom container API). Any model that meets the contract can be served, monitored, and governed by the platform — regardless of which framework trained it.

The CNCF's "Platforms for Cloud Native" white paper and the Backstage open-source developer portal are increasingly referenced in ML platform engineering discussions. Several large organizations are building their ML platform self-service layer on top of Backstage, using it as the UI/catalog layer over Kubeflow/MLflow/KServe infrastructure.

Platform engineering for ML means building golden paths, self-service, and opinionated defaults into your ML infrastructure — so data scientists can ship models without understanding Kubernetes, and the platform team can enforce governance without blocking experimentation.

cards.title: Platform Team vs ML Engineer — Division of Labor
cards.teaser: The platform team owns the paved roads; ML engineers drive on them. Getting this boundary right determines whether the platform accelerates or blocks ML delivery. A misdrawn boundary creates either a bottleneck (platform owns too much) or fragmentation (platform owns too little).

runs.text: In a well-structured ML organization, the platform team and ML engineering teams have distinct but overlapping responsibilities. The confusion arises at the boundaries.
Platform team owns:

items.text: Infrastructure reliability.
The Kubernetes cluster running KFP, the MLflow tracking server, the feature store online serving layer. SLAs for these are the platform team's responsibility.
The platform API surface.
The Python SDKs, CLI tools, and UI that ML engineers use. Breaking changes in platform APIs require versioning and migration support.
Security and compliance guardrails.
Data access controls, network policies, model approval workflows. These are enforced at the platform level so ML teams cannot accidentally violate them.
Cost visibility.
Chargeback/showback reporting. Idle cluster detection. Spot instance policies. ML compute is expensive; the platform team is responsible for making costs visible and providing tools to optimize them.

runs.text: ML engineer owns:

items.text: Model quality.
Feature engineering decisions, model architecture, offline evaluation. The platform provides the infrastructure; the ML engineer provides the judgment.
Production model health.
Responding to drift alerts from the platform's monitoring tools. Triaging degraded model performance. The platform raises the signal; the ML engineer owns the response.
Feature definitions.
Writing feature transformations, registering features in the feature store. The platform provides the store; the ML engineer provides domain knowledge about what the features should be.

runs.text: The anti-pattern: the platform team builds a system so opinionated that ML engineers must file tickets to the platform team for any deviation. This recreates the IT-request-queue bottleneck in an ML context. The platform should enforce non-negotiables (security, compliance) while leaving model development decisions fully with the ML engineer.

The platform team owns the roads and guardrails — reliability, security, cost tools. The ML engineer owns what they drive: model quality, feature decisions, production health. The platform enforces the must-haves; the ML engineer owns the judgment calls.

cards.title: The 2026 Platform Landscape — Convergence Around the Lakehouse
cards.teaser: By 2026, the ML platform market has converged on a common architectural pattern: the lakehouse as the data layer, MLflow as the experiment and registry standard, and a runtime-agnostic serving layer. The differentiation between vendors is narrowing toward UX, compute economics, and LLM tooling.

runs.text: The ML platform landscape of 2026 looks substantially different from 2019. Three convergence forces have reshaped it:

items.text: Lakehouse convergence.

Delta Lake, Apache Iceberg, and Apache Hudi have become the standard table formats for ML training data. All major platforms — Databricks, SageMaker, Vertex AI, Azure ML — now support at least one open table format natively, reducing data lock-in. The training data layer is increasingly portable.
MLflow as the tracking standard.

MLflow has become the lingua franca of experiment tracking and model packaging. SageMaker supports MLflow models natively. Vertex AI can serve MLflow models. Azure ML integrates with MLflow tracking. Databricks invented it. The experiment tracking layer is largely commoditized.
Serving runtime consolidation.

KServe, Triton Inference Server (NVIDIA), and vLLM (for LLMs) have become standard serving runtimes supported across platforms. A model packaged for KServe or Triton can be deployed on any platform that supports the runtime.

runs.text: Where differentiation remains:

items.text: LLM tooling
— prompt management, RAG pipeline orchestration, fine-tuning workflows, and evaluation frameworks for generative models are the primary battleground in 2025–2026.
Compute economics
— GPU and TPU availability, spot/preemptible instance reliability, and accelerator-specific optimizations (FlashAttention, quantization) vary significantly across clouds.
Developer experience
— the quality of the notebook experience, CLI tooling, and debugging workflows remains a meaningful differentiator as infrastructure commoditizes.

runs.text: The practical implication: platform decisions made in 2026 are more reversible than they were in 2019. Open table formats, MLflow, and portable serving runtimes mean that migrating between platforms no longer requires rewriting every model pipeline. Invest in portability-first abstractions and let compute economics drive platform selection over time.

By 2026, the ML platform market has converged: open table formats for data, MLflow for tracking and packaging, and standard serving runtimes. The remaining differentiation is LLM tooling, compute access, and developer experience — making platform choices more reversible than ever before.

cards.title: Platform Maturity Model — From Ad-Hoc to Managed to Self-Service
cards.teaser: ML platforms evolve through predictable maturity stages. Understanding where your organization sits on the maturity curve determines what to build next and what to buy — and prevents investing in Level 3 capabilities before Level 1 problems are solved.

runs.text: Most ML platform failures stem from trying to solve the wrong level of problem: building a sophisticated self-service platform before the organization has stable training pipelines, or adding feature stores before there are more than three models in production. The maturity model:

items.text: Level 0 — Ad hoc.

Models are trained locally and deployed by copying files to servers. No reproducibility, no monitoring, no shared infrastructure. Each model is a unique artifact owned by one person. The organizational symptom: "only Alice knows how to retrain the fraud model."
Level 1 — Managed.

A shared training environment (managed Jupyter, SageMaker notebooks, or Databricks). MLflow or equivalent for experiment tracking. A model registry. CI/CD for model retraining triggered by data or schedule. Monitoring via basic endpoint metrics. Most teams should be at Level 1 before building further.
Level 2 — Standardized.

A feature store eliminating training-serving skew. Standardized pipeline templates for common model types. Automated retraining triggered by drift alerts. Multi-team governance (RBAC on model registry, feature access controls). This is Michelangelo-tier.
Level 3 — Self-service.

A new ML engineer can take a project from data exploration to production model deployment without engaging the platform team. Golden paths cover the most common patterns end-to-end. Cost attribution is automatic. This is the Netflix Metaflow / Uber Michelangelo aspiration — achievable only with a dedicated platform team of 5+ engineers.

runs.text: The maturity model also guides the build-vs-buy decision across levels: SaaS platforms provide Level 1 and Level 2 capabilities out of the box. Level 3 self-service — with deep golden paths tailored to your organization's specific data systems and compliance requirements — is where in-house investment is often required even at organizations that otherwise use SaaS.

Platform maturity runs from ad-hoc (models only one person can retrain) through managed (shared tools, MLflow), standardized (feature stores, automated retraining), to fully self-service (any ML engineer ships a model end-to-end without platform team help). Solve each level before building the next.
